deu.34:1|num_moab|The land and people east of the Dead Sea, descended from the son of Lot’s elder daughter (Genesis 19:36–37). The name is often explained as “from father” (me-av), recalling that origin, but this is uncertain.

deu.34:1|num_nebo|A mountain in Moab from which the LORD showed Moses the promised land before he died (Deuteronomy 34:1–5), and a nearby town given to Reuben (Numbers 32:38). The meaning is uncertain; it is often linked to Nabu, a Babylonian god.

deu.34:1|num_pisgah|A ridge or summit in the mountains of Moab, where Balak took Balaam (Numbers 23:14) and Moses viewed the land “to the top of Pisgah” (Deuteronomy 34:1). The word probably means “peak” or “ridge,” and is usually written “the Pisgah” in Hebrew.

deu.34:1|num_jericho|A walled city west of the Jordan, across from Israel’s last camp “in the plains of Moab by Jordan near Jericho” (Numbers 26:3). The name may come from yareach, “moon,” or from a word for “fragrance”; it is uncertain.
deu.34:1|gen_dan_city|A town in the far north of the land, where Abram caught up with the kings who had taken Lot (14:14). It is named after the tribe of Dan, which later settled there.

deu.34:2|gen_naphtali|Jacob’s son by Bilhah, and the tribe that came from him. The name means “my wrestling”: Rachel said, “With great wrestlings have I wrestled with my sister, and I have prevailed” (30:8).

deu.34:2|gen_ephraim|Joseph’s second son in Egypt. The name means “fruitful”: “God hath caused me to be fruitful in the land of my affliction” (41:52). Later the name also means the tribe that came from him.

deu.34:2|gen_manasseh|Joseph’s firstborn son in Egypt. The name means “making to forget”: “God, said he, hath made me forget all my toil, and all my father’s house” (41:51). Later the name also means the tribe that came from him.
deu.34:2|gen_judah|Jacob’s fourth son, by Leah, and the tribe that came from him. The name means “praise”: “Now will I praise the LORD” (29:35).

1chr.25:1|ot2_asaph|A Levite appointed by David as a chief singer, who sounded the cymbals before the ark (15:17, 19; 16:5). 1chr.25:1|ot2_heman|A Levite, grandson of the prophet Samuel (6:33–38), who with Asaph and Ethan or Jeduthun led the temple music under David (15:17; 25:1–6). jsm.1:55|mos_moses|The prophet who led Israel out of Egypt, who “saw God face to face” in the vision recorded in the book of Moses (Moses 1:1–2). Exodus 2:10 explains the name as “drawn out,” because Pharaoh’s daughter drew him from the water; it may also echo an Egyptian word for “son.”

jsh.1:1|aof_jesuschrist|Jesus is the Greek form of Joshua (Yeshua), “the LORD saves,” as the angel told Joseph: “thou shalt call his name Jesus: for he shall save his people from their sins” (Matthew 1:21). Christ is Greek for “anointed one,” the same title as Messiah.

jsh.1:3|dc_joseph_sr|The Prophet’s father and the first Patriarch to the Church, told that his calling is “to exhortation, and to strengthen the church” (D&C 23:5). He is one who “sitteth with Abraham at his right hand” (D&C 124:19).

jsh.1:3|jsh_palmyra|The western New York village where the Smiths moved from Vermont when Joseph was “in my tenth year,” in “Ontario (now Wayne) county” (1:3). It is said to be named for the ancient city of Palmyra in Syria, whose name is usually linked to the palm tree.

jsh.1:3|jsh_manchester|The township in Ontario County, New York, next to Palmyra, where the great religious excitement began “in the second year after our removal to Manchester” (Joseph Smith—History 1:5) and near whose village the plates lay (1:51). The history gives no meaning for the name.

jsh.1:4|dc_joseph_sr|The Prophet’s father and the first Patriarch to the Church, told that his calling is “to exhortation, and to strengthen the church” (D&C 23:5). He is one who “sitteth with Abraham at his right hand” (D&C 124:19).

jsh.1:4|jsh_lucy|Joseph’s mother, whose maiden name was Mack, “daughter of Solomon Mack” (1:4), and who joined the Presbyterian church with Hyrum, Samuel Harrison and Sophronia (1:7). Lucy is a Latin name tied to lux, “light.”

jsh.1:4|dc_alvin|Joseph’s eldest brother, who died on 19 November 1823 (Joseph Smith—History 1:4, 56) and whom Joseph saw in the celestial kingdom in 1836, marveling that he had died before the gospel was restored (D&C 137:5–6). Alvin is an English name usually explained as “elf friend.”

jsh.1:4|dc_hyrum|Joseph Smith’s older brother, whom the Lord calls “my son” (D&C 11:23), later Patriarch to the Church (D&C 124:91–92) and killed with Joseph at Carthage Jail (D&C 135:1). Hyrum is a form of the Hebrew name Hiram, often explained as “my brother is exalted.”

jsh.1:4|dc_samuel_smith|Joseph’s younger brother Samuel Harrison Smith, one of the first baptized and often called the Church’s first missionary, told that his calling is “to exhortation” (D&C 23:4). Samuel is Hebrew, “God has heard” or “name of God.”

jsh.1:4|jsh_don_carlos|The youngest of the Smith brothers, listed among the family’s children in 1:4. The name is Spanish: Don is a title of respect and Carlos is Charles, from a Germanic word for “free man.”

jsh.1:11|jsh_james|The English form of Jacob. In Joseph Smith—History 1:11–13, 26 it is the author of the letter whose verse 1:5, “If any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God,” sent Joseph to pray; in JS—H 1:72 and D&C 7:7; 27:12; 128:20 it is the apostle James, who with Peter and John held the keys of the Melchizedek Priesthood.

jsh.1:24|paul|The Apostle Paul, first known by his Hebrew name Saul. Once a persecutor of Christians, he became the Church’s great missionary to the Gentiles and wrote most of the New Testament’s letters.

jsh.1:33|morm_moroni|Mormon’s son, who survived the last battle at Cumorah, finished his father’s record and abridged the Jaredite record as the Book of Ether (Mormon 8:1; Ether 1:1). He wrote the book of Moroni.

jsh.1:35|dc_urim|Sacred instruments for receiving revelation, whose Hebrew names are usually understood as “lights and perfections.” Joseph describes “two stones in silver bows” fastened to a breastplate and deposited with the plates (Joseph Smith—History 1:35).

jsh.1:36|dc_malachi|The last Old Testament prophet, whose name means “my messenger” (Malachi 3:1), and whose chapters 3 and 4 Moroni quoted to Joseph with changes (Joseph Smith—History 1:36–39). D&C 110:14 and 128:17 point to Malachi’s promise that Elijah would come before “the great and dreadful day of the Lord.”
jsh.1:38|priesthood|God's power and authority, given to act in His name.

jsh.1:38|dc_elijah|The Old Testament prophet taken to heaven without tasting death (D&C 110:13), whose name means “my God is the LORD.” Malachi promised he would come “before the great and dreadful day of the Lord” (D&C 2:1; Joseph Smith—History 1:38), and he appeared in the Kirtland Temple in 1836 to commit the keys of turning hearts (D&C 110:13–16).

jsh.1:40|dc_isaiah|The Hebrew prophet whose name means “the LORD saves,” whose chapters 11 and 52 are explained in D&C 113 and whose chapter 11 Moroni quoted to Joseph (Joseph Smith—History 1:40). D&C 128:19 quotes Isaiah 52:7, “How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of those that bring glad tidings.”

jsh.1:42|dc_urim|Sacred instruments for receiving revelation, whose Hebrew names are usually understood as “lights and perfections.” Joseph describes “two stones in silver bows” fastened to a breastplate and deposited with the plates (Joseph Smith—History 1:35).

jsh.1:46|mos_satan|From a Hebrew word meaning “adversary” or “accuser”; in Moses he is the one who offered himself as redeemer in the council in heaven but “sought to destroy the agency of man” and was cast down (Moses 4:1–4). He is “the devil, the father of all lies” (Moses 4:4), called Perdition (Moses 5:24) and Lucifer (D&C 76:26).

jsh.1:56|jsh_harmony|The town in Susquehanna County, Pennsylvania, where Joseph and Emma lived and much of the Book of Mormon was translated (Joseph Smith—History 1:56, 61–67). The name is simply the English word; no other meaning is documented.

jsh.1:56|dc_susquehanna|A river and county in northeastern Pennsylvania where Joseph and Emma lived at Harmony during the translation (Joseph Smith—History 1:61–62). D&C 128:20 names “the voice of Michael on the banks of the Susquehanna”; the name comes from a Native American name for the river, whose meaning is uncertain.

jsh.1:57|jsh_isaac_hale|Emma’s father, of Harmony, Pennsylvania, at whose house Joseph boarded (1:57) and whose family “were very much opposed to our being married” (1:58). Isaac is Hebrew, “he laughs.”

jsh.1:57|dc_emma|Emma Hale Smith, Joseph’s wife, whom he met while boarding at her father’s home and married in January 1827 (Joseph Smith—History 1:57–58). The Lord calls her “my daughter” and “an elect lady” and tells her to make a selection of hymns (D&C 25:1, 3, 11); Emma is a Germanic name usually explained as “whole” or “universal.”

jsh.1:61|dc_martin|A farmer from the Palmyra area who gave Joseph fifty dollars for his move to Pennsylvania and took copied characters to Professor Anthon (Joseph Smith—History 1:61–65). The Lord told him to “impart (his property) freely to the printing of the Book of Mormon” (D&C 19:26); the name Martin is often traced to the Roman god Mars.

jsh.1:61|jsh_palmyra|The western New York village where the Smiths moved from Vermont when Joseph was “in my tenth year,” in “Ontario (now Wayne) county” (1:3). It is said to be named for the ancient city of Palmyra in Syria, whose name is usually linked to the palm tree.

jsh.1:64|jsh_anthon|A classical scholar in New York City, “celebrated for his literary attainments,” to whom Martin Harris took characters copied from the plates (1:62–65). By Martin’s account Anthon tore up his certificate when told an angel had revealed the plates, and said of the sealed part, “I cannot read a sealed book” (1:65).

jsh.1:66|dc_oliver|The schoolteacher who came to Joseph Smith on 5 April 1829 and wrote most of the Book of Mormon as Joseph translated (Joseph Smith—History 1:66–67). He received the Aaronic Priesthood with Joseph from John the Baptist (JS—H 1:68–72) and was named “the second elder of this church” (D&C 20:3); the scriptures give no meaning for his name.

jsh.1:69|messiah|Hebrew for “anointed one.” Kings and priests in Israel were anointed with oil. The Messiah is the Anointed One God would send to save His people. Christ is the Greek form of the same title.
jsh.1:69|priesthood|God's power and authority, given to act in His name.

jsh.1:69|dc_aaron|Moses’ older brother and Israel’s first high priest; the lesser priesthood “is called the Priesthood of Aaron, because it was conferred upon Aaron and his seed” (D&C 107:13; Joseph Smith—History 1:69). The meaning of the name is uncertain.

jsh.1:69|dc_levi|Jacob’s third son and the priestly tribe, a name that sounds like “joined,” from Leah’s words, “Now this time will my husband be joined unto me” (Genesis 29:34). The Aaronic Priesthood stays “until the sons of Levi do offer again an offering unto the Lord in righteousness” (D&C 13:1; Joseph Smith—History 1:69).

jsh.1:70|dc_aaronic|The lesser priesthood, named for Aaron and holding “the keys of the ministering of angels, and of the gospel of repentance, and of baptism by immersion” (D&C 13:1; 107:20). “Levitical” is a second name, because its offices came through Levi’s tribe (D&C 107:1, 6).

jsh.1:72|dc_melchizedek|The king of Salem and priest of the most high God who blessed Abraham (Genesis 14:18–20); his name means “king of righteousness” (Hebrews 7:2). The higher priesthood is named for him “to avoid the too frequent repetition of” the name of the Supreme Being (D&C 107:2–4).

aof.1:2|mos_adam|The first man; in Hebrew adam means “man” or “mankind” and sounds like adamah, “ground,” the dust he was formed from (Moses 3:7). The Lord says, “the first man of all men have I called Adam, which is many” (Moses 1:34), and Moses 6:9 says God “called their name Adam,” meaning the man and the woman together.

aof.1:4|aof_jesuschrist|Jesus is the Greek form of Joshua (Yeshua), “the LORD saves,” as the angel told Joseph: “thou shalt call his name Jesus: for he shall save his people from their sins” (Matthew 1:21). Christ is Greek for “anointed one,” the same title as Messiah.

aof.1:10|dc_israel|The new name God gave Jacob and then his family and nation; Genesis 32:28 explains it as one who has striven with God and prevailed, though scholars debate whether it means “he strives with God” or “God strives.” In these scriptures Israel is also the covenant people being gathered: “the keys of the gathering of Israel” (D&C 110:11) and “the literal gathering of Israel” (Article of Faith 10).

aof.1:10|aof_tentribes|The ten northern tribes of Israel, carried away by Assyria about 722 BC (2 Kings 17:6), whose restoration Article of Faith 10 affirms. D&C 110:11 says Moses committed “the leading of the ten tribes from the land of the north,” and 133:26–34 describes their return.

aof.1:10|mos_zion|The Lord names Enoch’s people Zion “because they were of one heart and one mind, and dwelt in righteousness; and there was no poor among them” (Moses 7:18), and the city is “the City of Holiness, even ZION” (7:19), taken up to heaven (7:21, 69). Moses 7:62 promises another, “a New Jerusalem,” and Article of Faith 10 says Zion “will be built upon the American continent.”

aof.1:10|mos_newjerusalem|The holy city to be built in the last days, also called Zion: “an Holy City … it shall be called Zion, a New Jerusalem” (Moses 7:62), “a land of peace, a city of refuge” (D&C 45:66). Independence, Missouri, is its center place (D&C 57:1–3), and Article of Faith 10 says it will be built upon the American continent.

aof.1:13|paul|The Apostle Paul, first known by his Hebrew name Saul. Once a persecutor of Christians, he became the Church’s great missionary to the Gentiles and wrote most of the New Testament’s letters.
